title: Charge, current, voltage, resistance and circuits
blurb: Explain static charge, Coulomb's law and electric fields, then use Ohm's law, series and parallel rules and P = IV to solve circuit problems.
question: A space heater and a hair dryer share one household circuit, and the breaker trips. How much current does each draw, why does one appliance failing not shut off the other, and why do you get a shock from a doorknob in winter?

teach.body: Formally, electric charge is a property of matter that comes in two kinds, positive and negative, measured in coulombs (C); one electron carries −1.60 × 10⁻¹⁹ C. Like charges repel and unlike charges attract. In plain English: objects become charged when electrons move. Gain electrons and you are negative; lose them and you are positive. Protons stay put in the nucleus, and charge is never created or destroyed, only moved (conservation of charge).

teach.h: Three ways to charge an object

rows.label: Example
values: Charged rod near a grounded sphere

teach.caption: A charged object attracts a neutral one by polarizing it. Lightning and a doorknob spark are static discharges.

teach.body: F = kq₁q₂/r² (k = 8.99 × 10⁹ N·m²/C², given). Like gravity it is inverse-square: double the distance and the force falls to one fourth. Unlike gravity it can attract or repel. An electric field is force per unit charge (N/C). Field lines point away from positive charges and toward negative charges; closer lines mean a stronger field. Example: two charges repel with 12 N; double the distance and the force is 3.0 N.

rows.label: Examples
values: Metals, the human body, salt water
Rubber, plastic, glass, dry wood, air

teach.caption: Grounding drains excess charge to Earth through a conductor.

teach.body: Current I is the rate of flow of charge, I = q/t, in amperes (A); it needs a complete (closed) loop. Voltage V, in volts, is the energy per unit charge, the 'push' from a battery or outlet. Resistance R, in ohms (Ω), opposes current; it rises with wire length, falls with a thicker wire and rises with temperature in metals. Ohm's law: V = IR. Electric power P = IV = I²R = V²/R, in watts.

head: To find
Use
Example
teach.caption: Never I = VR or R = I/V. For a fixed resistor, current is proportional to voltage.
Parallel total is LESS than the smallest branch; two equal resistors in parallel give half of one. Household wiring is parallel.

items: Series: 2.0, 3.0 and 5.0 Ω on 20 V. R = 10 Ω, I = 2.0 A everywhere; across the 5.0 Ω: 2.0 × 5.0 = 10 V.
Parallel: 3.0 Ω and 6.0 Ω. 1/R = 1/3 + 1/6 = 1/2, so R = 2.0 Ω. On 12 V: 4.0 A + 2.0 A = 6.0 A total.
Power: a lamp draws 0.50 A at 120 V. P = 0.50 × 120 = 60 W.
Energy: a 100 W lamp on for 10 h uses 1,000 Wh = 1.0 kWh (power × time).

teach.body: Rosa, a respiratory therapy applicant, runs a 1,500 W heater and a 1,200 W hair dryer on one 120 V circuit. The heater draws 1,500 ÷ 120 = 12.5 A and the dryer 1,200 ÷ 120 = 10 A. The outlets are in parallel, so the currents add to 22.5 A, more than the circuit's 15 A breaker allows, and it opens. Household outlets supply alternating current (AC); batteries supply direct current (DC).

teach.text: Positive charging is losing electrons, not gaining protons. Coulomb's law is inverse-SQUARE. Ohm's law is V = IR, not I = VR. Series resistances add; parallel totals are smaller than the smallest branch. Current is not used up along a series circuit. A thicker wire has LESS resistance. Watts measure power; watt-hours measure energy. Houses are wired in parallel.

items: Like charges repel, unlike attract; charging moves electrons; charge is conserved.
F = kq₁q₂/r² (inverse-square); field lines run from + to −.
V = IR; I in amperes, V in volts, R in ohms; resistance rises with length, falls with thickness.
Series: same current, R adds. Parallel: same voltage, total R below the smallest branch.
P = IV = I²R = V²/R; energy = P × t (kWh on bills).

summary: You can now explain how objects become charged, apply Coulomb's inverse-square law and read electric field lines. You can also use Ohm's law, combine resistors in series and parallel, and calculate electric power and energy for household circuits.

A.q: A glass rod rubbed with silk becomes positively charged. What happened to the rod?
options: It gained protons from the silk
It gained electrons from the silk
It lost electrons to the silk
A.why: An object becomes positive by losing electrons. The silk gained them and became negative by the same amount.

whyNot.0: Protons stay in the nuclei; only electrons move during charging.
whyNot.1: Gaining electrons would make the rod negative.
whyNot.3: Charge is conserved: rubbing moves electrons, it does not create charge.

A.q: A positively charged sphere is brought near a second positive sphere, and then near a negative sphere. What happens in each case?
A.why: Like charges (positive and positive) repel; unlike charges (positive and negative) attract.

whyNot.1: Reverses the rule for like and unlike charges.
whyNot.2: Unlike charges attract; they do not repel.
whyNot.3: Like charges repel; they do not attract.

A.q: What is the SI unit of electrical resistance?
A.why: Resistance is measured in ohms (Ω): R = V ÷ I.

whyNot.0: The ampere is the unit of current.
whyNot.1: The volt is the unit of voltage (potential difference).
whyNot.2: The watt is the unit of power.

B.q: A 6.0 V battery drives a current of 0.50 A through a lamp. What is the lamp's resistance?

whyNot.0: Multiplies V by I (6.0 × 0.50); that gives power in watts, not resistance.
whyNot.3: Adds voltage and current, which have different units.

B.q: Three 6.0 Ω resistors are connected in parallel. What is their combined resistance?
B.why: 1/R = 1/6 + 1/6 + 1/6 = 3/6 = 1/2, so R = 2.0 Ω, less than any single branch.

whyNot.0: Adds them as if in series.
whyNot.1: A parallel total is less than the smallest branch, not equal to it.
whyNot.2: Stops at 1/R = 0.50 and forgets to take the reciprocal.

B.q: Which of these is a good electrical conductor?
B.why: Salt water contains dissolved ions that carry charge, so it conducts well.

whyNot.1: Rubber is an insulator, used to coat wires.

C.q: A 3.0 Ω and a 6.0 Ω resistor are connected in series to an 18 V battery. What is the voltage across the 6.0 Ω resistor?

whyNot.1: 18 V is the whole battery voltage; series resistors share it.
whyNot.2: 6.0 V is the voltage across the 3.0 Ω resistor (2.0 × 3.0).
whyNot.3: Splits the voltage equally; series voltages divide in proportion to resistance.

C.q: The voltage across a fixed resistor is doubled. What happens to the current through it and the power it uses?
C.why: I = V/R, so I doubles. P = V²/R, so P rises by 2² = 4.

whyNot.0: Power depends on V², so it quadruples, not doubles.
whyNot.1: With R fixed, more voltage drives more current, not less.
whyNot.3: Power rises with both current and voltage, so it must change.

C.q: Two point charges attract each other with a force of 20 N. If one charge is doubled and the distance between them is also doubled, what is the new force?
C.why: Doubling one charge gives × 2; doubling the distance gives ÷ 2² = ÷ 4. 20 × 2 ÷ 4 = 10 N.

whyNot.0: Counts the doubled charge but leaves out the distance change.
whyNot.2: Treats the distance change as ÷ 2 (1/r), which would cancel the doubled charge.
whyNot.3: Applies the distance change but leaves out the doubled charge.

reteach.title: Water in pipes
reteach.question: If a circuit were plumbing, what would voltage, current and resistance be?

blocks.body: Picture a pump pushing water around a loop of pipe. The pump's push is the voltage. The amount of water passing a point each second is the current. A narrow or long section of pipe is a resistance: it cuts the flow for the same push, just as V = IR says. Pipes one after another (series) carry the same flow through each. Pipes side by side (parallel) each get the full push and their flows add, so the total resistance drops.

blocks.text: Water is not used up as it passes a narrow pipe, and current is not used up as it passes a resistor. The same current returns to the source.

explain.body: Rubbing two materials moves electrons from one to the other. One ends up negative, the other positive by the same amount.

test.q: A balloon rubbed on a child's hair becomes negatively charged. What is the hair's charge afterward, and why?
options: Neutral: no charge moved to it
test.why: Electrons moved from the hair to the balloon. Having lost electrons, the hair is positive by the same amount.

whyNot.0: The balloon gained the electrons, not the hair.
whyNot.2: Protons do not move; the hair is positive because it lost electrons.
whyNot.3: The hair lost the electrons the balloon gained, so it is charged.

explain.body: Lines show the push on a positive test charge: out of positive charges, into negative charges. Closer lines, stronger field.

test.q: Which way do the electric field lines around an isolated positive charge point?
test.why: A positive test charge is pushed away from a positive charge, so the field lines point outward.

whyNot.0: Lines point inward toward a negative charge.
whyNot.1: Circular lines describe the magnetic field around a current, not an electric field.
whyNot.3: Parallel lines describe the uniform field between two charged plates.

explain.body: In series a single break stops all current. In parallel each branch has its own path.

test.q: In an old string of holiday lights, one burned-out bulb makes the whole string go dark. What does this show?
options: The bulbs are wired in parallel
The bad bulb uses up the current
The voltage across the rest rises
The bulbs are wired in series
test.why: In series there is a single path, so one open bulb breaks the loop and current stops everywhere.

whyNot.0: In parallel the other bulbs would stay lit.
whyNot.1: Current is not used up; the broken bulb opens the only path.
whyNot.2: With the loop broken, no current flows, so the other bulbs get no working voltage.

explain.body: Power (W) is a rate. Energy = power × time; on bills it is in kilowatt-hours (1 kWh = 1,000 W for 1 h).

test.q: A 60 W lamp is left on for 5.0 h. How much energy does it use?

whyNot.1: Divides power by time (60 ÷ 5.0) and labels it kWh.
whyNot.2: 300 is the answer in watt-hours, not kilowatt-hours.
whyNot.3: Slips a decimal place converting 300 Wh to kWh.
